title: How would you design an autocomplete / type-ahead suggestion service (prefix lookups via a trie or an edge-ngram index, ranking suggestions by popularity/recency, debouncing client requests, caching hot prefixes, and bounding latency to a few ms)?
shortTitle: How would you design an autocomplete / type-ahead suggestion service

s1_definition.profdef: An autocomplete service returns ranked completions for a partial query in a few milliseconds. The core data structure is a trie (prefix tree) or an edge-ngram inverted index that makes prefix lookups near-instant, each terminal node carrying the top candidate completions pre-ranked by a popularity and recency score. The client debounces keystrokes to avoid a request per character, hot prefixes are cached in memory or Redis, and the whole path is latency-bounded because suggestions must appear faster than the user types the next character.
s1_definition.analogy: When Rajesh types into National Bank of India's search box, as he types "ho" the box should instantly suggest "home loan", "home insurance", "housing scheme". Imagine a smart index where all the bank's known search phrases are filed by their first letters, so under "ho" there is already a short pinned list of the most popular phrases starting with those letters. The moment Rajesh types "ho", the clerk flips straight to that pre-written list, no searching required. The box also waits a fraction of a second after he stops typing before asking (debounce), so it does not fire off a request for every single letter, and the most common prefixes are kept on the clerk's desk (cache) for instant answers.
s1_definition.oneliner: Pre-rank the top completions under each prefix in a trie or edge-ngram index, debounce keystrokes, cache hot prefixes, and keep the whole lookup under a few milliseconds.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An autocomplete service returns ranked completions for a partial query in a few milliseconds. The core data structure is a trie (prefix tree) or an edge-ngram inverted index that makes prefix lookups near-instant, each terminal node carrying the top candidate completions pre-ranked by a popularity and recency score. The client debounces keystrokes to avoid a request per character, hot prefixes are cached in memory or Redis, and the whole path is latency-bounded because suggestions must appear faster than the user types the next character.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When Rajesh types into National Bank of India's search box, as he types "ho" the box should instantly suggest "home loan", "home insurance", "housing scheme". Imagine a smart index where all the bank's known search phrases are filed by their first letters, so under "ho" there is already a short pinned list of the most popular phrases starting with those letters. The moment Rajesh types "ho", the clerk flips straight to that pre-written list, no searching required. The box also waits a fraction of a second after he stops typing before asking (debounce), so it does not fire off a request for every single letter, and the most common prefixes are kept on the clerk's desk (cache) for instant answers.

**One line to remember:** Pre-rank the top completions under each prefix in a trie or edge-ngram index, debounce keystrokes, cache hot prefixes, and keep the whole lookup under a few milliseconds.

sections.s2_technical:
Why prefix lookups need a special structure. Autocomplete answers "given this prefix, what are the best full phrases that start with it". Doing that with a database LIKE 'ho%' is a prefix scan that can use an index but still returns and ranks many rows per keystroke, which is too slow and too frequent. The right structures are a trie or an edge-ngram index. A trie stores characters along paths from the root, so walking down h then o lands you at the node for "ho", and from there you read pre-computed top suggestions. An edge-ngram index, used by Elasticsearch, pre-tokenizes each phrase into all its prefixes (h, ho, hom, home, home l, and so on) and indexes them, so a prefix query becomes an ordinary exact-term lookup. Both turn prefix search into a direct traversal or lookup rather than a scan.

Pre-ranking the completions. Users want the best suggestions, not any suggestions. Each phrase has a score combining popularity (how often it is searched or chosen) and recency (recent trends weighted higher, so a newly popular scheme surfaces). You precompute, at each trie node or for each prefix, the top K completions already sorted by this score, so answering a query is just reading that small pinned list, not sorting at query time. The score is updated in the background as new usage data arrives; you do not recompute on the request path.

Debouncing client requests. If you fire a request on every keystroke, typing "home loan" sends nine requests, most of them wasted because the user keeps typing. The client debounces: it waits a short idle period, typically 150 to 300 milliseconds after the last keystroke, before sending a request, and cancels the in-flight request if a new keystroke arrives. This cuts request volume dramatically and only asks when the user pauses. The client also discards out-of-order responses so a slow earlier response does not overwrite a newer one.

Caching hot prefixes. A small number of prefixes account for most traffic, like "ho", "lo", "fd". You cache the pre-ranked suggestion list for hot prefixes in an in-memory cache or Redis with a short TTL, so the common queries never even hit the trie service. This both lowers latency and sheds load. The cache is keyed by prefix and holds the ready-to-return list.

Bounding latency. The hard requirement is that suggestions appear before the user types the next character, so you target single-digit milliseconds end to end. You achieve this by keeping the trie in memory, returning pre-ranked lists without query-time sorting, caching hot prefixes, limiting suggestions to a handful (top 5 to 10), and keeping payloads tiny. You also cap the work: if a prefix has a huge subtree, you never traverse it at query time because the top-K is already pinned at the node.

Handling scale and updates. The trie or index is built offline from historical query logs and product catalogs, then loaded into memory on each suggestion server. Usage events (what users searched and clicked) stream in and periodically update the scores and the pinned top-K, so rankings stay fresh without blocking reads. For very large vocabularies you shard the trie by first letters across servers. Personalization, if needed, blends a user's own recent searches with the global list, but the global pre-ranked list is the fast default.

The senior nuance is the read-heavy, precompute-everything mindset. Autocomplete is overwhelmingly reads at brutal latency targets, so you move all the expensive work (ranking, sorting, aggregation) to an offline or background path and make the request path a trivial pinned-list read. Fuzzy prefix matching for typos can be layered on, but it is more expensive, so you apply it carefully, often only when the exact prefix yields too few results.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India has a search box. As Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) type, it suggests popular phrases like products and services.

Problem 1 — a request per keystroke overwhelmed the service. Typing "home loan" fired nine backend calls, most immediately stale, and the service buckled under the volume. This is why the client debounces, waiting until the user pauses before asking.

Problem 2 — suggestions were slow and unranked. The old version ran LIKE 'ho%' and returned results in alphabetical order, so the most popular "home loan" was buried. This is why we use a trie with pre-ranked top-K completions by popularity, so the best phrase appears first in milliseconds.

Problem 3 — the same hot prefixes hit the service repeatedly. "ho" was queried thousands of times a minute. This is why we cache hot prefixes so repeated common queries are served instantly from memory.

The mini-project builds a runnable demo: a `Trie` that inserts phrases with popularity scores and maintains a pre-ranked top-K at each node, a `SuggestionService` with a hot-prefix cache and a latency measurement, and a `Debouncer` simulating client-side debounce. It inserts banking phrases, serves ranked suggestions for "ho" and "lo", shows the cache hit on a repeated prefix, and shows debounce collapsing many keystrokes into one request.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: seven banking phrases with popularity scores; queries "ho", "ho" again, "lo", and a debounced "home".

Step 1: Each phrase is inserted into the trie. For "home loan" (score 950), the characters h, o, m, e, space, l, o, a, n create a path, and at every node along that path the phrase is considered for that node's top-K. So the node for "ho" now has "home loan", "home insurance", "housing scheme", "home loan top-up" in its pinned list, pre-sorted by score.

Step 2: Query "ho" walks h then o to reach the "ho" node and reads its pinned top-K directly. No sorting happens at query time, it was done at insert. Results come back ranked: "home loan" (950), "home insurance" (600), "housing scheme" (300), "home loan top-up" (200). The service measures the latency in microseconds, well under the 5 ms budget, and caches the list for "ho".

Step 3: Query "ho" again. The service checks the cache first, finds the fresh list, and returns it without touching the trie. This is the hot-prefix cache hit, even faster and offloading the trie.

Step 4: Query "lo" walks l then o and reads its top-K: "loan against property" (700), "loan calculator" (500). Ranked by popularity, not alphabetically.

Step 5: The client types h, o, m, e quickly. The debouncer accumulates them and, only after the user pauses for the debounce interval, fires a single request for the prefix "home" instead of four separate requests. The service then returns suggestions for "home". This is how nine keystrokes become one or two requests.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ── Build (offline / background) ──
  Query logs + catalog
    │ phrase + popularity + recency score
    ▼
  Trie insert: pin top-K at EVERY prefix node
    "ho" node → [home loan 950, home insurance 600, housing 300, ...]

  ── Request path (few ms) ──
  Rajesh types h,o,m,e
    │ client DEBOUNCE 200ms → one request "home"
    ▼
  SuggestionService
    │ PrefixCache.get("home")  ──HIT──▶ return pinned list  (fastest)
    │          │ MISS
    │          ▼
    │   Trie.suggest("home")  → walk h-o-m-e → read node.topK (O(K), no sort)
    │          │
    │          ▼  cache.put("home", list)  (TTL 60s)
    ▼
  Response: [home loan, home insurance]  (ranked by popularity)

  ── Background score updates ──
  usage events → recompute scores → refresh pinned top-K (never on read path)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
An autocomplete service has one brutal requirement: it must return ranked completions for a partial query faster than the user types the next character, so I design the whole thing as a read-optimized, precompute-everything system with a single-digit-millisecond budget. I never answer it with a database LIKE 'ho%', because even though a prefix wildcard can use an index, it still returns and ranks many rows on every keystroke, which is both too slow and far too frequent. Instead I use a trie, a prefix tree where walking down the characters h then o lands directly at the node for that prefix, or an edge-ngram index where each phrase is pre-tokenized into all its prefixes so a prefix query becomes an ordinary exact-term lookup. Both turn prefix search into a direct traversal rather than a scan.

The key trick is that I pre-rank the completions and pin them at each node. Each phrase has a score combining popularity, how often it is searched or chosen, and recency so trending phrases surface, and I precompute the top handful of completions already sorted at every prefix node. So answering a query is just reading that small pinned list in order of K, with no sorting at request time, because the ranking was done offline and refreshed in the background from usage events. This is what fixed our problem where LIKE returned results alphabetically and buried the most popular home loan.

On the client side I debounce keystrokes. Firing a request per character means typing home loan sends nine requests, most immediately stale, which overwhelmed our service. Instead the client waits a short idle period, around two hundred milliseconds after the last keystroke, before sending one request, cancels any in-flight request when a new key arrives, and discards out-of-order responses so a slow older response cannot overwrite a newer one. That collapses many keystrokes into one or two requests. I also cache the pre-ranked list for hot prefixes like ho and lo in memory or Redis with a short TTL, so the common queries never even reach the trie, which both lowers latency and sheds load.

To hit the latency budget I keep the trie in memory, return pinned lists without query-time sorting, cache hot prefixes, limit results to the top five or ten, and keep payloads tiny, and I never traverse a large subtree at query time because the top-K is already pinned at the node. The structure is built offline from historical query logs and the catalog, loaded into memory on each suggestion server, and usage events stream in to periodically refresh the scores and pinned lists without ever blocking reads. For a huge vocabulary I shard the trie by first letters across servers, and I can layer in fuzzy prefix matching for typos, but carefully, usually only when the exact prefix returns too few results, because fuzzy is more expensive.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that autocomplete is a read-heavy precompute problem: I store phrases in a trie or edge-ngram index with the top-ranked completions pinned at every prefix node, I debounce keystrokes and cache hot prefixes, and I move all ranking to an offline or background path so the request is a trivial pinned-list read that returns ranked, popularity-aware suggestions in a few milliseconds.
